The birth of Charles VI's first son in September 1386 was a significant dynastic event. The Aragonese court's congratulatory letter, sent in early November, reflects normal diplomatic timing for such news to travel and responses to be prepared.

1. **Joan I (Rex Johannes)**: King of Aragon from 5 January 1387 upon the death of his father Pere III el Cerimoniós. These documents date from the first month of his reign. The styling "Rex Johannes" without "Infans" confirms his assumption of full royal authority.

2. **Petrus de Beniure (Pere de Beniure)**: Royal secretary who served both Pere III and Joan I. His continued presence in the subscription confirms administrative continuity during the transition.

4. **Bernat de Millano**: Identified as lieutenant of the alguacil (chief enforcement officer). The alguacil was responsible for criminal justice and arrest warrants.

**Document 2 - The Criminal Investigation**: The reference to "crimes committed against our firstborn daughter" is highly significant. Joan I's firstborn daughter was **Joana** (born 1375), though she died in 1407. The flight of a person accused of crimes against the infanta and her apparent refuge in the County of Empúries suggests either a serious offense at court or a political dimension to the case. The use of the alguacil's lieutenant indicates criminal rather than civil proceedings.

**Document 3 - Municipal Negotiations**: The document addresses "prohomens" (probi homines), the leading citizens or magistrates of a municipality. The reference to "justifications" and negotiations about realms and lands suggests discussions about privileges, taxation, or the recognition of Joan I as the new king—common immediately after a succession.

### Geographic References

- **Barcelona**: Royal residence and location of chancery at this date
- **County of Empúries (Comtat d'Empúries)**: Semi-autonomous county in northern Catalonia, bordering France

### Persons Identified:

1. **Joan I (John I of Aragon)**: Became king on 5 January 1387 upon the death of his father Pere III (Peter IV "the Ceremonious"). The transition from "Infans" to "Rex" visible in this register reflects this succession.

The date "xxviiii dies de febrer" (29 February) in 1387 is calendrically impossible, as 1387 was not a leap year. This represents either:
- A scribal error for 28 February (the actual last day)
- Use of the Roman calendar convention where dates were counted backwards from the Kalends of March (in which case "ante diem III Kalendas Martii" could be rendered confusingly)
- A simple slip of the pen (xxviiii for xxviii)

### Register Context:
This folio shows the transition period immediately following Joan I's accession. Documents from January 1387 onward should bear his title as King rather than Infante Lieutenant, which matches what we observe.

### Main Text

**[1. General Supplication]**
Your humble and devoted son John, by the grace of God King of Aragon, supplicates Your Holiness that you deign to kindly receive and graciously hear the petitions written below, with appropriate clauses and executory provisions in [standard] form. *[Granted]*

**[2. Regarding Sardinia and Corsica]**
First, since the same King holds from the Roman Church the Kingdoms of Sardinia and Corsica in fief under a certain tribute or census to be paid annually, and on account of the wars that have existed and continue to exist in the said Kingdom for many years past, and on account of the rebellion of the said [Judge of] Arborea, and also on account of the great and unbearable expenses which he has incurred for the subjugation of the said Kingdom, he has ceased to pay the said tribute or census of the Kingdom for some years past, since he was unable [to do so] with his subjects — may Your Holy Lordship deign to remit to him the gross [arrears] of all past time. And since the said trust, with all labors and services, and [the King] has [continued the work] of his predecessor the late lord King [Pere III] who drove out the greater [part] of the tyrants, and he has aided, sustained, and continues to sustain [the effort] for the Roman Church — may the same Holy Lordship deign to concede and grant by special grace to the said prince, in the name of the said Kingdom, to the same King and his successors in perpetuity, the said tribute and all allodial and feudal right of the Roman Church over the aforesaid [lands], so that the same Kingdoms may be free and exempt from the census of the said King and his perpetual successors, as an allod [free from all lordship], from all payment of tribute or census and any other burden whatsoever sought, and exempt. *[Granted]*

**[3. Regarding Chapel Benefices]**
Likewise, so that the same King may better be able to have suitable clerics for his chapel and household, may Your same Holy Lordship deign to grant graciously to the King and his successors in perpetuity that in each cathedral church of the said King's lands [he shall have] the right of patronage over one dignity and one office and two canonries with prebends, and in each diocese of the said King's dominion, four rectorships or likewise curacies; so that the said King and his successors, whenever [such benefices] become vacant, may present suitable persons to the ordinaries for the said dignities, offices, canonries with prebends, and likewise curacies, once [chosen] in perpetuity, or [persons] to be chosen by themselves. And the ordinaries [shall be bound] to confer the same upon those suitable persons so presented. *[Granted]*

**[4. Regarding Marriage Dispensations]**
Likewise, since for any dispensation to be obtained concerning a marriage written below, it is necessary to have recourse to the Roman Curia and to obtain the said graces — may Your Holy Lordship deign to commit to the Archbishop of Tarragona and the Bishop of Barcelona, who now are and who shall be for the time being, and to grant them full power, that for any marriage to be contracted within their diocese between any persons who are or were on either side in the third or more remote degree of consanguinity or affinity, they may freely dispense by apostolic authority — namely, the said Archbishop and Bishop within his province, and the said Archbishop of Tarragona and the other [Bishop] in all lands under royal jurisdiction, if it seems [appropriate] to them. *[Granted]*

**[5. Regarding Tithes]**
Likewise, may Your same Holiness deign to grant to the King the tithes of churches and ecclesiastical benefices of his dominion for eleven years, so that with these [funds] and the aid of his subjects he may be able to recover the patrimony of the Kingdom of Aragon, [and] primarily of the said Kingdoms of Sardinia and Corsica, [which has been] alienated. *[Granted]*

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons
- **Petrus Rex Aragonum / Pere III el Cerimoniós (Peter IV)**: Joan I's father, who died 5 January 1387. References to his "indisposition" (*indispositio*) refer to his final illness. The "antipope Bartholomew" insult refers to Urban VI, whom the Crown of Aragon rejected in favor of Clement VII (Avignon obedience).

- **Bartholomeus Antipapa**: This is Urban VI (Bartolomeo Prignano), whom the Avignon party considered an antipope. The Crown of Aragon supported Clement VII.

- **Ozargarita de Loria / Countess of Terranova**: This appears to be **Margarita de Lauria** (or de Loria), descendant of the famous admiral Roger de Lauria. The family held extensive properties in Valencia and Sicily. "Terranova" refers to lands in Sicily.

- **Altea**: A barony in the Kingdom of Valencia, on the Mediterranean coast. This property was tied to the primogeniture and subject to restrictions on alienation.

- **The Cardinalate request** (Item 2): This is a significant political request—Joan I is asking the Pope to elevate two of his nominees to the College of Cardinals, strengthening Aragonese influence in the Avignon curia.

### Context
These *capitula* represent diplomatic instructions for an embassy to Pope Clement VII at Avignon, likely carried by the ambassadors mentioned in earlier folios. The requests cover:
1. Absolution from censures incurred during Pere III's reign
2. Elevation of Aragonese prelates to the cardinalate
3. Removal of entail restrictions on the Altea barony
4. Confirmation of benefice holders appointed during the interregnum/royal illness

The reference to *bandositates* (feuds/factions) reflects the chronic problem of clerical benefice disputes fueling noble faction violence in the Crown of Aragon.

This document represents a series of *capitula* (petition articles) that Joan I's ambassadors would present to Pope Clement VII at Avignon. The petitions address several concerns:

1. **Extension of liturgical privileges**: The king requests that the privilege of hearing divine services during interdict (granted to him personally) be extended to his queen, Violant de Bar.

2. **Protection of native clergy**: A major concern is the infiltration of foreign (non-Aragonese) clergy into benefices within the Crown of Aragon, particularly through papal provisions. This was a common complaint throughout the Avignon period.

3. **Restrictions on cardinals**: The petitions seek to limit the number and type of benefices that cardinals can hold within the Crown's territories—a frequent source of tension between secular rulers and the papal curia.

4. **Saracen threat**: The reference to "Saracens" (Muslims) suggests concern about the security implications of non-resident benefice-holders in frontier regions.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified

1. **Joan I of Aragon** (r. 1387–1396): Acceded to the throne upon the death of his father Pere III "el Cerimoniós" on 5 January 1387. These letters, dated 10 and 17 January 1387, are among the earliest of his reign, explaining the title "El Rey Daragon" without the fuller royal titulature that would become standard.

2. **Pere de Santcliment** (Petrus de Sanctoclemente): A prominent Aragonese knight and royal councillor, frequently employed in diplomatic missions during the reigns of Pere III and Joan I.

3. **Ramon de França**: Doctor of laws (legum doctor) and director of the chancery (director cancellarii) of the Kingdom of Aragon. An important legal officer of the Crown.

4. **Pere de Çesplugues**: Royal councillor; the Çesplugues (or Desplugues) family was prominent in Aragonese court service.

5. **Joan de Santa María**: Described as "sacristan cellero" (sacristan and cellarer) in the Kingdom of Aragon — likely connected to the royal chapel administration.

6. **Francesc ça Costa**: Chancery scribe who physically drafted the Latin letter.

7. **Pere de Beniure**: Royal secretary (secretarius) who registered both documents. The register cover confirms he served as secretary from October 1386 through October 1387.

### Recipients

1. **Bishop of Palermo** (Episcopo Panormitano): Per marginalia. In 1387, the Bishop of Palermo was likely Niccolò de Agrigento or a successor; Sicily was closely connected to the Crown of Aragon.

2. **Master of Rhodes** (Magistro Rotensis): The Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller (Order of St. John), based at Rhodes. In 1387, this was **Juan Fernández de Heredia** (1377–1396), himself an Aragonese and major figure in late medieval diplomacy.

### Context: The Embassy to Rome

Both letters concern the same diplomatic mission: an embassy to Pope **Clement VII** at the Avignon Curia (the "Roman Curia" in loyalist terminology, as Aragon recognized the Avignon papacy during the Great Schism). The embassy's purpose involved:
- Affairs touching the Crown and the Church
- Matters concerning royal benefices and ecclesiastical appointments
- Likely negotiations regarding the ongoing Schism

The letters request that the recipients give full credence to the ambassadors and assist in expediting their mission.

- **Violant de Bar as Regent**: The subscription "Domine Regina" confirms this is issued by Queen Violant de Bar acting as locumtenens (lieutenant) for the Infante Joan during his father Pere III's final illness or after the latter's death on 5 January 1387.

  - **Ismail** = Isma'il I (r. 1314-1325) or Isma'il II (r. 1359-1360)

- **Francí Morge**: A messenger or envoy between the crowns of Aragon and Granada—an interesting figure in cross-confessional diplomacy.

- **Condolence Diplomacy**: This letter exemplifies the elaborate courtly conventions maintained between the Christian kingdoms of Iberia and the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, including expressions of shared grief and religious formulas adapted for interfaith correspondence (notably, the reference to the deceased as a "Catholic prince" and "faithful King" may be diplomatic courtesy or a scribal formula).

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

**[Folio 26 recto]**

Most dear and most beloved brother King. We, the King of Aragon, send you many greetings, as to one for whom we desire and wish as much life, health, and honor as we desire for ourselves.

Know, most dear and most beloved brother King, that we have received the letter that you sent to us through the honored father in Christ the Bishop of Dufmet[?] and the Archdeacon of Truyo[?], your ambassadors, and we have fully understood the credentials that the said ambassadors have explained to us on your behalf, very extensively and well.

Which [credentials], in summary, contain four matters:

**First**, that we, out of regard for the great and good bonds of kinship that exist between the two of us, and in aid and support of you, should issue a formal challenge [desafiassemos] to the Duke of Lancaster.

**Second**, that between the two houses of France and yours, the old confederations should be reformed and new alliances made.

**Third**, that we should provide you aid of certain galleys and men-at-arms.

**Fourth** and last, that by way of loan, or in another manner, we should assist you with some quantity of money.

To which four matters, and firstly to the first two, we respond that although we love you cordially, most dear brother, and your house, to such a degree that we feel your honor as our own, and consequently we have abiding affection and will toward the defense and good estate of that [house]—nevertheless, since neither we nor our predecessors have ever been accustomed to undertake or wage wars, nor [make] peace or alliances with any kings or princes, without full deliberation, counsel, and consent of our people and subjects, with whom and with whose aid and [counsel] on various matters and affairs we must act, and [since] our predecessors at all times have conducted the said wars [in this manner], we cannot at present, nor would it be expedient, to make the challenge and alliances abovesaid.

Rather, of necessity for this purpose, we must await a parliament or general Cort to be convened by us with our said subjects. We intend to convene this parliament or Cort as soon as we can, since even now, by reason of the illness that we have had, our person is not disposed for this purpose. And in the said Cort we intend to propose and discuss the matter, and bring it to the best conclusion we can, in such a manner that you, most dear brother, may reasonably be satisfied thereby.

However, according to what we have understood, within a few days ambassadors of my most dear brother the King of France are to be with us to negotiate, among other matters, concerning the said alliances. And thus if there is any means by which we may now find it expedient to accomplish those [alliances], we shall write to you clearly about it by further letters.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Eixemen Pérez de Corella** (Jimeno Pérez de Corella): Noble Valencian lineage; appointed Governor of Cagliari and Alghero (the two principal royal territories in Sardinia). His appointment represents Joan I's effort to stabilize royal administration in Sardinia after the turbulent period of the Arborea rebellion.

**Guillem Gralla and Narnau Frigola**: Ambassadors (*missatgers*) sent by the *prohoms* and municipal authorities of Cagliari to the royal court in Barcelona. Their mission evidently sought military reinforcement and administrative reform for the island.

**Pere de Beniure** (Petrus de Beniure): Royal secretary (*secretarius*) under Joan I. He is identified in the register title as the responsible scribe for this entire register (October 1386 – October 1387).

### Places

**Caller/Cagliari**: The principal city of royal Sardinia and seat of the governor. The "Castle" (*Castell*) referred to is likely the Castello district of Cagliari, the fortified upper city that was the administrative and defensive heart of the Aragonese presence.

**Alguer/Alghero**: The second major Aragonese stronghold in Sardinia, on the northwestern coast, refounded as a Catalan settlement after 1354.

### Context

This letter dates to August 1387, approximately eight months after Joan I's accession (January 1387). The references to the island being "so long afflicted" (*tan longament fatigada*) by administrative abuses and the urgent need for a governor with "force and power" reflect the chronic instability of Aragonese Sardinia. The Giudicato of Arborea, under Eleonora d'Arborea, controlled much of the island and posed a constant military threat to the Crown's coastal enclaves. Joan I's dispatch of Eixemen Pérez de Corella represents an attempt to reassert royal authority and reassure loyal subjects.

And because the inquisition mandated by you, and which [proceeding] uniquely elaborates merit in such a manner [for] the completion and public welfare as set forth above, is pleasing [to us]. We grant for the swifter dispatch of this inquisition, it pleases us and we wish you, by the said inquisitors or judges, granting divine [aid] in the present [matter], by long [experience] and authority of time, to re-examine [witnesses] at one leap, being present and instituting [proceedings], from among those knights or crowd, or to examine [them] at diverse times.

### Persons:

1. **Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387–1396):** This document dates from early in his reign. He became king upon the death of his father Pere III el Cerimoniós on 5 January 1387. The signature "Rex Iohannes" confirms he is now ruling in his own right rather than as lieutenant.

2. **Sancho Ocártiz de Biota:** A member of the Aragonese nobility serving as acting Governor (*tenens vices gubernatoris*) of Aragon. The Ocártiz family were prominent in the administration of the kingdom. Biota is a town in the Cinco Villas region of Aragon.

3. **Count of Urgell:** Almost certainly Jaume I d'Urgell (1321–1389), also known as Jaume el Dissortat ("the Unfortunate"). He was involved in numerous territorial disputes with the Crown during this period.

### Places:

1. **Barbastro:** Important city in the Somontano region of Aragon, strategically located between the Pyrenees and the Ebro valley. Urban conflicts between factions were common in Aragonese cities during this period.

2. **Jaca:** Principal city of the Aragonese Pyrenees, former capital of the early medieval kingdom. The reference to "affairs of Jaca" suggests the governor was dealing with similar urban disorder there.

3. **Fraga:** Town on the Cinca River in eastern Aragon, near the border with Catalonia. The jurisdictional dispute mentioned here reflects the complex overlapping claims in the frontier zone between Aragon and the County of Urgell.

4. **Barcelona:** Royal residence and administrative center of the Crown of Aragon.

### Administrative Context:

The register title (*Curie sigilli secreti locumtenencie infantis Joannis*) indicates these documents were issued under the secret seal during Joan's lieutenancy, though by March 1387 he was already king. The transition from lieutenant to king in January 1387 is reflected in the signing style.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

**Joan I ("lo Rey Darago")**: Joan I of Aragon (r. 1387-1396), son of Pere III el Cerimoniós. The dating of these documents (27 April 1387) places them in the first months of his reign—his father died on 5 January 1387. The reference to his upcoming coronation in Aragon is significant; Joan I was crowned at Zaragoza on 3 April 1388.

**Pere de Beniure (P° de Beniure)**: Royal secretary ("escrivà de manament") who handled documents sealed with the secret seal during this transitional period. The register title confirms his role: "Curie sigilli secreti locumtenencie infantis Joannis."

**Gau de Radonella**: Messenger of the "prohomes" (notables) addressed in Document 2. The name suggests Catalan origin; "Radonella" may refer to a place in Catalonia or the Balearics.

**Thomas Romeu**: A courier or minor official used to transmit documents to the ambassadors at the Roman Curia.

### Places and Contexts

**Roman Curia**: The embassy to the Roman Curia in 1387 was crucial during the Western Schism. Joan I, like his father, supported the Avignon papacy (Clement VII). The ambassadors were likely negotiating recognition, ecclesiastical preferments, or crusade matters.

**The Chamois Request**: Joan I's personal request for chamois hides (one large, one small) is a characteristic example of how medieval rulers used diplomatic channels for personal commissions. Chamois leather was prized for its softness and was used for gloves, linings, and fine garments. The request "the largest you can find and the smallest there be" suggests a specific purpose—possibly for contrasting items or for the king and a child.

**Coronation Plans**: The upside-down text references preparations for the coronation ("celebrar nostra benaventurada coronacio"). Joan I's coronation was delayed until April 1388 due to various political and logistical factors.

### The "Petit Anell" Subscription

The formula "subsignada ab nostre petit anell" indicates authentication with the king's small personal ring rather than the great seal or even the standard secret seal. This marks the document as a personal rather than official communication—appropriate for a request about chamois hides.

This letter represents Joan I's early efforts to consolidate power following his accession. ### Persons

1. **Clement VII (Avignon Pope)**: Robert of Geneva, Avignon Pope (1378–1394) during the Great Western Schism. The Crown of Aragon under Pere III and Joan I supported the Avignon obedience. The reference to papal bulls granting ecclesiastical tithes (*decimas*) reflects the financial arrangements between the papacy and the Crown.

2. **Johan de Murcos, citizen of Barcelona**: Appointed as general receiver (*receptor generalis*) for the collection and distribution of ecclesiastical tithes. His designation as a *fidolis de domo nostra* (faithful member of our household) indicates he was a trusted royal servant. The office of tithe receiver was financially significant and required both administrative competence and loyalty.

3. **Joan, Primogenitus (Duke of Girona)**: The future Joan I of Aragon, at this time (1386–1387) serving as lieutenant-general of the realm during the final illness of his father Pere III el Cerimoniós. Pere III died on 5 January 1387, so documents from early 1387 in this register may still use the "primogenitus" intitulation before the new royal style was adopted.

4. **Petrus de Benyure**: Royal secretary (*secretarius*), as noted in the register's title. He was responsible for expediting documents under the secret seal during Joan's lieutenancy.

### Context

This document relates to the **papal tithe grants** (*decimas*) conceded by Clement VII to support the Crown of Aragon. Such grants were common during the Avignon papacy, particularly to monarchs supporting the Avignon line. The appointment of a centralized receiver for the "third part" (*tercia pars*) suggests a division of tithe revenues — possibly between the Crown, the Church, and other parties, or between different territorial administrations.

The mention of the **secret seal** (*sigillo secreto*) indicates this was an administrative document processed through the camera (private chancery) rather than the public chancery.

- **Date context**: The document dates from early 1387, shortly after Joan I's accession (January 1387) following the death of Pere III el Cerimoniós. This mandate likely represents the new king's early efforts to address longstanding problems of public order.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons
- **Joan I of Aragon**: Became king on 5 January 1387 upon the death of his father Pere III el Cerimoniós. These documents date from July 1387, six months into his reign.
- **Pedro de Beniure**: Royal secretary (secretari) who managed the privy seal correspondence. His name appears consistently in the iussio clauses throughout this register.
- **Governor of Aragon (Gubernator Aragonum)**: The royal representative responsible for justice and public order in the Kingdom of Aragon. At this date, the office was likely held by Juan Ximénez Cerdán or a similar noble.

### Places
- **Barbastro**: Important market town in the Aragonese pre-Pyrenean region (Somontano). Its annual fair was a significant commercial event attracting merchants from across the kingdom and the mountain valleys.
- **"Exas montanyas" (those mountains)**: Refers to the Aragonese Pyrenean valleys, often areas with endemic noble feuding (bandositats).

### Events & Context
- **Bandos/Bandositats**: The endemic factional violence between noble lineages in Aragon and the Pyrenean regions. These feuds frequently disrupted commercial and civil life, requiring royal intervention.
- **Fair of Barbastro**: Medieval fairs enjoyed special legal protections (conductu, paz de feria). Violence during fairs was a serious offense requiring royal response.
- **The Governor's mission**: The documents reveal the Governor was already in the mountains dealing with disputes but was being given discretionary orders about attending the fair—reflecting the king's need to balance peacekeeping priorities.

- The mention of "affers de la pau" (affairs of the peace) directly references these negotiations
- The governor of Sardinia being sent as a credentialed envoy indicates high-level diplomatic activity

**[Responses to Articles - continuation]**

To the 7th article: the same, and as to the preceding.

To the 8th and 9th articles: because they ought not to be touched [i.e., they should remain unchanged].

To the 10th article: the same as to the preceding.

To the 11th and 12th articles: the same.

Regarding the 13th article: it has already been informed verbally by the Lord King who is [reigning] today.

Item, to the first article concerning the retentions made by the said Lord King: in order that the form of the said article [be followed], because the quantity for which the realm ought to be left [as guarantee] should be expressed verbally by the Lord King to the said Mossèn Pere Perç.

Item, the 2nd article: because the furnishing [of provisions/equipment] ought to be comprised with refinement and [despite] difficulties, for this reason let it be left to the free judgment of Mossèn Pere Perç.

Item, the 3rd article: because it stands well, for if anyone suffers damage or grievance, the Lord King will make him swear orders; let the article itself be added to the response to the said article.

Item, the 4th article: because it is good.

In this matter the Lord King wills that since Mossèn Dalor de Lige has, through a loyal recommendation, taken in trust from [?] the said Lord King, in perpetual and good memory during the war of Sardinia, all the goods, immovable and movable, of the said Mossèn Dalor, which have been left to him and purchased by Jurge, and [the King] promises that they shall be returned to him, or the value of those [goods], as estimated at the judgment of seven persons, that is, two [chosen] by each party as electors.

### Seal Reference

The document was issued under the **sigillum secretum** (privy seal), as indicated in the corroboratio and consistent with the register's title (*Curie sigilli secreti*). The privy seal was used for administrative correspondence and less formal royal acts, as distinct from the great seal (*sigillum majus*) used for solemn diplomas.

The recipient of Document 4 is **Levon V** (or VI by some counts), the last king of Armenian Cilicia (r. 1374-1375). After the fall of Sis to the Mamluks in 1375, Leo was taken captive to Cairo. By 1387, Leo was residing variously in Castile, France, and traveling between courts. The Crown of Aragon had long-standing connections to the Kingdom of Armenian Cilicia through crusading ties and Mediterranean commerce. This letter appears to concern:
- Health of Pere III (who died January 1387 - this reference may be retrospective or conventional)

> Governor, [we have received] your letters and the others that you sent us with the bearer of this present [letter], and we thank you for the news from Castile that you made known to us, and we command you that whenever you learn of other news, you should send them to us first.

Nevertheless, we hope in the mercy of God that within a few days we may ride and enter into that which befits our honor and service and defense and good governance of our Kingdoms. ## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

1. **Joan I of Aragon ("El Rey")**: Joan I became king on 5 January 1387 upon the death of his father Pere III el Cerimoniós. At this date (August 1387), he had been king for approximately seven months. The register title indicates it began during his lieutenancy (locumtenencia) and continued into his reign.

2. **Sancho Martínez de Biota**: A trusted official serving as portantveus (lieutenant/deputy) of the Governor of Aragon. The Governor of Aragon was a major office responsible for military and judicial administration in the kingdom. The portantveus was his principal deputy.

3. **Duke of Montblanc**: This is Joan I's brother, Martí (the future Martí I, r. 1396-1410). He held the title Duke of Montblanc from 1387. His journey "toward the regions of Berga" in the Pyrenean frontier zone relates to the defense concerns discussed.

4. **Llop de Peramplea (Lupus de Peramplea)**: A royal familiar (household member) serving as diplomatic envoy. Sent to the papal curia, indicating diplomatic business with Clement VII (the Avignon pope recognized by Aragon) or his cardinals.

5. **Pere de Beniure**: The royal secretary (secretarius) who authorized these documents on behalf of the king. Named in the register description as the primary secretary for this volume.

### Places

1. **Castile**: The neighboring kingdom; news from Castile was of strategic importance given frequent tensions and the complex dynastic politics of the period.

2. **The frontier mountains and passes**: The Pyrenean frontier between Aragon and France/Navarre, requiring vigilant defense.

3. **Berga**: A town in the Catalan Pyrenean foothills (modern province of Barcelona), a strategic point for frontier defense.

4. **Barcelona**: The royal residence and seat of chancery at this time.

### Context

The documents reflect Joan I's concerns about frontier defense while dealing with health issues that prevented him from traveling ("within a few days we may ride"). The reference to his "absence" being "greatly displeasing" suggests he was confined, possibly by illness (Joan I was known for periods of ill health).

The Latin letters to the Pope and Cardinal relate to ongoing Crown of Aragon diplomatic relations with the Avignon papacy during the Western Schism. Aragon recognized Clement VII (1378-1394).

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons

1. **Cardinal of Viviers (Cardenal de Viuenna)**: Likely Jean de Brogny (Johannes de Brogniaco), who was connected to Avignon and active in papal diplomacy during the Great Schism. The see of Viviers was in the Avignon sphere of influence.

2. **Infanta Dona Johana**: Likely Joana of Aragon, daughter of Pere III. Marriage negotiations with the Holy Roman Emperor were a recurring diplomatic theme.

3. **Emperor of Germany (Emperador d'Alamanya)**: Reference to the Holy Roman Emperor. In 1386-1387, this would be Wenceslaus IV (King of the Romans from 1376, but never crowned Emperor). The "schismatic" reference connects to the Great Western Schism.

4. **King of France (Rey de França)**: Charles VI, who supported the Avignon papacy. The Crown of Aragon maintained careful diplomatic relations with France, especially regarding papal politics.

5. **Sant Pare (Holy Father)**: The Avignon Pope Clement VII, whom the Crown of Aragon recognized during the Schism.

### Context

This document reflects the complex diplomacy of the Great Western Schism (1378-1417). The Crown of Aragon recognized the Avignon papacy, and Pere III/Joan I had to navigate marriage alliances carefully to avoid alienating either the Pope or the King of France while dealing with the "schismatic" King of the Romans who supported the Roman Pope.

The marginal notation "Dominus Rex mandauit pro domino Episcopo Valentie" suggests involvement of the Bishop of Valencia in these negotiations.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Context
This document relates to Joan I's reorganization of municipal government in Mallorca. The pragmatic sanction established new procedures for electing the jurats (municipal magistrates) and consellers (councillors) of the City of Mallorca.

### Key Persons Identified

**Knights (Cavallers):**
- **Johan de Mora**: Member of the prominent Mora family of Mallorca
- **Thomas de Garç**: Likely of the Garci/Garcés family
- **Bernat de Febrer**: Febrer was a notable Mallorcan lineage
- **Berenguer de Galiana** and **Jacme de Galiana**: Members of the Galiana family, prominent in Mallorcan affairs

### Institutional Context
The **vigilia de Sancta Maria d'Agost** (14 August, eve of the Assumption) was a traditional date for municipal elections in the Crown of Aragon. Joan I's pragmatic sanction of 5 August 1387 reformed the electoral system, likely in response to factionalism or to consolidate royal control over municipal appointments.

### Title "Mossen"
The prefix "Mossen" (from "mon senyor") indicates knightly status—these were members of the military nobility of Mallorca qualified to serve as jurats.

### Document 1: Royal Mandate

> **John**, [by the grace of God, firstborn of the King of Aragon, Duke of Girona, Count of Cervera], etc., to our faithful disbursement officer **Guillem Callet**, greeting, etc.
>
> Since certain men, outsiders [*forenses*], persons of the *locaria* of Cervera, come before our court demanding on their behalf that [monies/obligations] be repaid to them by virtue of the positions [*posicionibus*] which they made to the Lord King of splendid memory, our father, for the redemption of services [*servicia*] commuted from certain censuses against the *Junquarios*, inasmuch as our father, according to the complaint, acted against them contrary to the custom of the armed peoples, as is contained in our [records] which [were presented] to our said father [in] the Chapter for the Chapter of Catalonia, [and] our procurators, to whose expertise [the matter] has been recognized by us...
>
> [W]e commit and command that, having recognized the obligations and payments made by the said men firstly concerning their own redemption, [distinct] from others whom you represent in our name, you not only exact [what is owed] but also [determine] by what [means] and how much was taken by them from the said operations, not only [for] our court and [our] magnates, to recover according to that to which they are obligated.
>
> According to the form of the obligation made by them, which through them [was deserved?], [we command] you or any deputy in your place [to act] as public judge. And concerning what is not intended by you, make and confirm apportionments. And if they should be in delay, immediately through officials cause to be brought [them] to [justice], so that execution may be vigorously carried out, by which alone [payment] from private persons customarily is made.
>
> To all of which, we [command] each and every official and porter of your [jurisdiction] that concerning the said execution, he act insofar as he shall be required by you.
>
> And concerning the price, [we command] you that through our faithful councillor and vicar, you respond to our [representatives] otherwise remaining.
>
> **Given at Barcelona**, under our seal as [stated] before, **a day in July, in the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1387**. Alfonsus received [this for registration].

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons
- **Infante Joan / Joan I**: The issuer, Joan (1350–1396), firstborn of Pere III el Cerimoniós. At this date (July 1387), his father Pere III had died (January 1387), making Joan now King Joan I. The register title notes documents from this period span his transition from infante to king.

- **Guillem Callet**: Royal disbursement officer (*expensor*), a financial official responsible for payments and accounting.

- **Archbishop of Zaragoza**: In 1387, this was **García Fernández de Heredia** (archbishop 1383–1411), an important figure in Aragonese ecclesiastical and political affairs.

- **"Regina fur madre" (Queen mother)**: Refers to **Sibil·la de Fortià**, fourth wife of Pere III, who was queen mother after Pere's death. The marginal note indicates the document relates to her interests via a procurator from Tàrrega.

### Events
- **Bandos of Uclés and Torres**: Reference to factional feuds (*bandositats*) involving noble families, possibly related to the Order of Santiago (whose main house was in Uclés) and territorial disputes in Aragon/Castile.

- **French Companies (*companyes de ffrança*)**: This is a significant reference to the **routier companies** or **Free Companies** — bands of mercenary soldiers (many French) who plagued the Iberian Peninsula throughout the 1380s. These companies had been involved in Castilian civil wars and periodically crossed into Aragonese territory. The concern expressed about them "passing into Castile" via the frontiers of Aragon reflects ongoing diplomatic and military anxieties about these dangerous armed bands.

- **Chapter of Catalonia / Capitol**: Reference to the Corts or parliamentary assembly of Catalonia where grievances (*greuges*) were presented and redressed.

### Places
- **Cervera**: Important town in Catalonia, seat of a county held by the Aragonese crown.
- **Zaragoza**: Capital of the Kingdom of Aragon, seat of the archbishop and municipal government.
- **Barcelona**: Location where the document was issued; primary seat of the royal chancery.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Joan I's Health and the Regency Context
Document 2 contains a significant historical detail: the king mentions being in "buena conualescen[ci]a" (good convalescence) and unable to ride ("no podemos cavalgar"). Joan I was known to have suffered health problems. His inability to travel personally to Aragon in August 1387 is noteworthy, as he had only become king in January 1387 following the death of Pere III (IV).

### The "Bandos" in Aragon
The reference to "los bandos no han peleyado" (the factions have not fought) relates to the endemic factional violence in Aragonese cities, particularly Zaragoza, during this period. The urban "bandos" or "bàndols" were noble-led factions whose rivalries frequently erupted into violence. The king's correspondence shows active royal concern with maintaining peace among these factions.

### The "Companies of France"
The previous folio's reference to "companyes de ffrança" (French companies) relates to the routier companies (mercenary bands) that plagued the Iberian kingdoms during this period, particularly in the aftermath of the Castilian civil wars and continuing French conflicts.

### Secretarial Staff
- **Pere de Beniure**: Royal secretary active during the transition from Pere III to Joan I
- **Bernat de Jonquero**: Another royal secretary appearing in Joan I's early reign

### The "First Year of Our Reign"
Document 2's dating formula "d[e] n[uest]ro [regno]" (of our reign) confirms this is from the reign of Joan I, whose regnal years began January 1387.

This document reflects Joan I's efforts to secure ecclesiastical preferment for his wife's family at the Avignon papal court (Clement VII). The Catalan postscript represents the king's personal voice, bypassing chancery formalism. The claim that the king's hand is too unsteady to write himself (but that this note should be treated as autograph) is a common diplomatic fiction, though Joan I's genuine ill health makes it plausible here.

1. **The Free Companies returning from Castile:** This document relates to the movements of mercenary companies (routiers) who had been engaged in the Castilian civil wars and were now seeking passage through the Crown of Aragon to return to France. To Esperandeu Cardona and Pere de Beniure, the poverty and doubt which have deeply moved you both—after the *pragmàtica* [royal ordinance] that we recently made concerning the government of the City was protested and requested by you—these are the doubts:

The first [doubt] is: why was the schedule (*cedula*) of the names of the twenty-four *prohoms* [worthy men] that we selected for the said government made on paper and [then] on parchment, after the said *pragmàtica* so ordains.

The second doubt concerns an erasure (*rasura*) that exists in the said schedule, in the column of the names of the *maclers* [butchers/guild members], that is, between [the names of] Jordi Brondo and Gabriel de Smena, in which erasure nothing has been written.

To the first doubt, since it seems reasonable, we make this explanation: that the said schedule was made on paper and not on parchment, and this because we were not well disposed afterwards to sign the aforesaid. However, we did so nevertheless, although reluctantly. Appropriately, however, and for this reason it was necessary to supply a subscription with permission of our signet ring, which permission we do not customarily [give], and because in the case or other pretext not formed on paper and also solely in erasure and integrity of a person. And this change from parchment to paper does not create law nor remove it, nor does it change the substance of the above-said *pragmàtica*. And since it is to satisfy malice, we placed ourselves within the great [assembly] to present a schedule on parchment, subscribed, as was suspected. And a court with the said signet ring, and we would have given it on paper and high on parchment.

To the second doubt, we say that it is without reason, for since nothing is written in the erasure, there was no need to doubt. But so that you may understand what is doubted, and so that you may know that in order to make me certain—from the hand of whom the said schedule was copied—I found in the space where the said erasure is, Johan Damato, who made the copy, that there were thirty-one names, and the said Johan Damero has given me the remainder—that is, left blank in the lines placed after the name of the said Jordi Brodo, which begins "in the case that Lop Lofia de Tauler" [?]. And already to remove all suspicion, nothing was written in this space, nor any of the other names in the part of which you should know are in the other columns where the said signet ring was placed in the aforesaid sign, which thing was so evident that nothing had been transported nor said nor changed.

And for this reason it was ordered that the entire said schedule should be thus as it was written by the hand of the said [scribe], so that they would not have occasion to place any doubt therein. We have not believed that certain of these [persons] among some of our household, that some of the council of this city create doubt, and those who are summoned to the bank [of magistrates]...

### Persons:
- **Joan I** (r. 1387-1396): Became King of Aragon in January 1387 upon the death of his father Pere III el Cerimoniós. This document dates from September 1387, during his first year as king.

- **Pedro de Benyure** (Pere de Beniure): Royal secretary who served under both Pere III and Joan I. Identified in the register as the secretary through whom documents were expedited 1386-1387.

- **Batlle General de Aragó**: The chief royal fiscal and administrative officer for the Kingdom of Aragon, responsible for managing royal patrimony and executing crown commands.

- **Alfonso Cano**: Royal messenger (*portador*) entrusted with delivering this letter and apparently with taking physical possession of contested castles.

- **Garcia Lopez**: Recipient of Document B; an Aragonese noble ("Mosen" = *miles*, knight).

- **"El duch"**: Likely refers to the Duke of Montblanc (the Infant Martí's title before becoming king) or another ducal figure in the royal family.

### Places:
- **Lorca**: Town in the Kingdom of Murcia, then under Castilian sovereignty but with Aragonese interests. Mentioned as a location for signing/authentication.

- **Çaragoça** (Zaragoza): Capital of the Kingdom of Aragon; seat of the Justicia de Aragón and important judicial institutions.

- **Aragins**: Castle where Gil de Sada was previously imprisoned; likely a royal fortress used for detention.

- **Barcelona**: Location of the royal court at the time of issue.

### Historical Context:
This document reveals tensions over castle custody in Aragon during the early months of Joan I's reign. The refusal of Gil de Sada to surrender a castle to the Batlle General suggests resistance to royal authority or disputes over jurisdictional boundaries between royal and seigneurial power. The involvement of the "Jutges de Çaragoça" (Judges of Zaragoza) indicates the matter had a judicial dimension, possibly involving the distinctive Aragonese fueros (customary laws).

- Recovering alienated royal patrimony
- Documenting feudal obligations
- Asserting royal fiscal rights
- Preventing usurpation of Crown lands

The ordering of capbreus was a characteristic action of new monarchs seeking to consolidate their fiscal position, making this document's timing (months after Joan I's accession) historically significant.

## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified:

1. **Joan I of Aragon (Rex Johannes):** Succeeded his father Pere III el Cerimoniós on 5 January 1387. The presence of "Rex Johannes" rather than "Infans Johannes" confirms this document dates after the accession.

2. **Pere de Beniure/Benyure:** Royal secretary (escrivà de manament) serving under Joan I. He is recorded as active throughout this register (1386-1387).

3. **Mossèn Johan de Bellvís (Belluis):** A Valencian nobleman involved in factional violence. The Bellvís family was prominent in the Valencian nobility.

4. **Mossèn Rodrigo de Miranda:** Valencian noble, apparently opposed to Pere de Centelles.

5. **Mossèn Pere de Centelles:** Member of the powerful Centelles lineage, one of the leading noble families of Valencia, frequently involved in the bandositats of the period.

6. **Rodrigo de Borja:** Possibly an ancestor or relative of the Borja (Borgia) family, already prominent in Valencia.

7. **Jacme Ferrer, Salman de Fluvià:** Participants in the Valencian factional conflicts.

### Historical Context:

This document addresses the endemic problem of **bandositats** (factional feuds) among the Valencian nobility in the late 14th century. These private wars between noble lineages created persistent disorder in the Kingdom of Valencia. The Crown repeatedly attempted to suppress such conflicts through the governor (Governador) and his lieutenant (portantveus), appealing to the fueros (Valencian law) and threatening royal intervention.

The mention of "desafiaments" (formal challenges/defiances) indicates the formalized nature of these conflicts, where nobles would issue public challenges before engaging in violence.

### Persons Identified:

This is a **bandejament** or royal proclamation requiring all subjects in Valencia to:
- Recognize the death sentence against Vilarigut
- Refuse to aid or harbor him

- Face penalties of forfeiture if they assist the condemned

The phrase "condemnat a mort et omnia bona eius nostro fisco adjudicata" reflects the standard dual penalty of capital punishment and confiscation of goods for major crimes (often treason or crimes against the royal person).

## 5. HISTORICAL NOTES

1. **Albaida and Carricola:** Towns in the present-day comarca of Vall d'Albaida, Valencia. These were significant lordships in the medieval Kingdom of Valencia.

2. **Fuero of Valencia:** The reference to "juxta ipsius Regni forum" invokes the Furs de València, the compilation of laws and customs governing the Kingdom of Valencia, which had specific provisions regarding feudal tenure, allodial property, and redemption rights.

3. **Queen Violant de Bar:** The "illustrious Queen our most dear consort" is Violant de Bar (1365-1431), wife of Joan I, who maintained her own household with officers like the Villarçanio mentioned here.

4. **Direct and Allodial Lordship:** The document concerns the distinction between feudal tenure (held in fief with obligations) and allodial ownership (held freely without feudal obligations). The supplicant seeks to convert feudal holdings to full allodial property.

5. **Pedro de Beniure:** The secretary who handled documents under Joan I's privy seal during this period (October 1386-October 1387), as indicated by the register's cover sheet.

6. **Gonzalvo/Gonzalo Gubertar:** A military commander (captain of militia) in the Kingdom of Valencia; the exact identification requires further research in Valencian military records.

## 3. ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### Document 1

To the Most Serene Prince Charles, by the grace of God King of the French, our most dear kinsman. Joan, by the same grace King of Aragon, etc., [sends] greetings and prosperous success according to [your] wishes.

Most Serene Prince and most dear kinsman: We are sending the Noble and beloved councillor and chamberlain of ours, Raimon de Perellós, knight, Viscount of Roda, to your [presence] regarding certain affairs of ours and of the said Court to be advanced, and we [have] fully informed him. Therefore [we ask] the said excellency attentively that concerning those things which the said lord [envoy] shall report to you on our behalf and concerning our state, you deign to give full and credulous faith to all these things. Furthermore, Lord, since [we seek] the good disposition toward contemplation and regard of you and ours, and whatever things possible to you, Lord, we shall have done [or] accepted with full confidence, responding. Given at Barcelona under our secret seal, the 27th day of October, in the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1387.

Historical Notes:
## 4. HISTORICAL NOTES

### Persons Identified

**Raimon de Perellós (Raymund de Perilionibus)**
- Viscount of Roda (Perellós)
- Knight (miles), Royal Councillor (consiliarius), and Chamberlain (camerlengus) to Joan I
- Member of the prominent Perellós family of Roussillon
- Famous for his 1397 journey to St. Patrick's Purgatory in Ireland, which he documented in his *Viatge al Purgatori de Sant Patrici*
- Frequently employed as a diplomatic envoy due to his connections with the French court (his family held lands in French-influenced territory)

**Charles VI of France (Karolus Francorum Rex)**
- King of France 1380-1422
- Called "the Beloved" and later "the Mad"
- Joan I's "consanguineus" (kinsman) through complex Capetian-Aragonese marriage connections
- In 1387, Charles VI was still actively governing before the onset of his mental illness (which began in 1392)

**Joan I of Aragon (Johannes Rex Aragonum)**
- King of Aragon 1387-1396
- Succeeded his father Pere III (IV) "el Cerimoniós" on 5 January 1387
- Known for his cultural patronage and love of music ("el Caçador" - the Hunter)
- The documents date from October 1387, early in his reign

### Context

These letters of credence were issued to support a diplomatic mission to the French court. The exact nature of the "arduous affairs" is not specified in these credential letters, but in late 1387, several matters concerned Aragon-France relations:
- The ongoing Western Schism (Aragon supported Clement VII in Avignon; France also supported Clement)
- Commercial and territorial matters in Roussillon and Languedoc
- Possible marriage negotiations or dynastic concerns

The use of the secret seal (sigillum secretum) indicates these were matters handled through the king's private chancery rather than the formal public chancery.
